facts.text: Franz starts for school late and fears M. Hamel will question him on participles.
A Berlin order requires schools in Alsace and Lorraine to teach only German.
M. Hamel announces that this is the class's final French lesson.
Village elders occupy the normally empty back benches to honour M. Hamel and their language.
M. Hamel wears his special green coat, frilled shirt, and embroidered cap.
Franz suddenly regrets neglecting his French books and lessons.
M. Hamel calls French the world's most beautiful, clearest, and most logical language.
At noon M. Hamel writes 'Vive La France!' on the blackboard and dismisses the class by gesture.
Saheb-e-Alam is a barefoot ragpicker from Seemapuri whose family left Dhaka after storms destroyed their fields.
For Seemapuri's ragpickers, garbage is both daily survival and a source of hopeful discoveries.
Saheb searches garbage instead of attending school, although he says he wants to study.
Saheb later earns eight hundred rupees and meals at a tea stall but loses his carefree independence.
Mukesh belongs to a Firozabad family traditionally engaged in making glass bangles.
Children work in hot, dark bangle furnaces that damage their eyesight.
Poverty, caste, middlemen, police, bureaucrats, and politicians keep bangle makers trapped in exploitation.
Mukesh resolves to become a motor mechanic and learn to drive a car.
A childhood wave at a California beach first gives William Douglas an aversion to water.
Douglas chooses the YMCA pool because the Yakima River is dangerous.
An older boy throws Douglas into the pool's nine-foot-deep end.
Douglas repeatedly tries to spring from the bottom but nearly drowns before being rescued.
The incident creates a lasting fear that spoils his fishing, canoeing, boating, and swimming.
An instructor trains him with a belt, pulley, breathing exercises, kicking, and coordinated strokes.
Douglas tests himself by swimming two miles across Lake Wentworth to Stamp Act Island.
After swimming across Warm Lake and back, Douglas knows he has conquered his fear.
The peddler survives by selling wire rattraps, begging, and petty theft.
He imagines the world as a rattrap whose baits are riches, food, shelter, and comfort.
A lonely crofter shelters him and reveals thirty kronor earned from his cow's milk.
The peddler steals the crofter's thirty kronor and becomes lost in the forest.
At Ramsjo Ironworks, the ironmaster mistakes him for an old regimental comrade, Captain von Stahle.
Edla Willmansson persuades the frightened stranger to spend Christmas at the manor.
Even after his identity is exposed, Edla lets him remain as a respected guest.
The peddler leaves the stolen money for the crofter, a rattrap for Edla, and a note signed Captain von Stahle.
Rajkumar Shukla persistently asks Gandhi to visit Champaran and help indigo sharecroppers.
British landlords compel peasants under the tinkathia system to plant indigo on fifteen percent of their land.
Synthetic indigo leads landlords to demand compensation for releasing peasants from the planting agreement.
Gandhi refuses an official order to leave Champaran and accepts the legal penalty for disobedience.
A crowd of peasants gathers at the Motihari courthouse, revealing their new courage.
An official inquiry committee includes Gandhi and investigates the peasants' grievances.
The landlords agree to refund twenty-five percent of the illegally exacted money.
Gandhi also promotes village education, sanitation, health, and self-reliance in Champaran.
Asokamitran recalls his years at Gemini Studios in Madras.
The make-up department uses large quantities of Pancake brand make-up under incandescent lights.
An office boy in the make-up department dreams of literary and acting success.
The office boy wrongly blames Subbu for his own frustrated career.
Kothamangalam Subbu is the studio's cheerful, loyal, resourceful No. 2.
The legal adviser is nicknamed the opposite because his recording ends an actress's career.
Gemini Studios hosts the Moral Re-Armament army's plays Jotham Valley and The Forgotten Factor.
Years later, the narrator identifies the mysterious English visitor as poet Stephen Spender.
The interview has become a common form of journalism since its invention a little over a century ago.
Celebrities such as V. S. Naipaul, Lewis Carroll, Rudyard Kipling, and H. G. Wells express distrust of interviews.
Denis Brian argues that an interviewer can reveal vivid truths about contemporaries.
Mukund Padmanabhan interviews Umberto Eco, a university professor, semiotician, and novelist.
Eco calls the empty intervals in life 'empty spaces' or interstices and uses them productively.
Eco describes his scholarly writing as having a playful and personal narrative quality.
Eco considers himself a university professor who writes novels on Sundays.
The Name of the Rose succeeds enormously despite its serious medieval history, theology, and metaphysics.
Sophie dreams of owning a boutique, becoming an actress, or becoming a fashion designer.
Jansie expects both girls to work at the biscuit factory after school.
Sophie's family lives modestly, and her father works as a labourer.
Sophie tells Geoff that she met Irish football prodigy Danny Casey in the arcade.
She later adds that Casey promised to meet her again and give her an autograph.
Geoff is Sophie's quiet older brother, and she imagines joining his unknown world.
The family watches Casey score the winning goal for United.
Sophie waits alone by the canal, but Casey never arrives because the meeting is her fantasy.
Kamala Das sets the poem during a Friday morning drive from her parent's home to Cochin airport.
The poet's sixty-six-year-old mother dozes beside her with her mouth open.
The mother's ashen face reminds the poet of a corpse.
The poet turns away from the painful recognition of her mother's ageing.
Young trees seem to sprint past the moving car.
Merry children spilling from their homes contrast with the elderly mother.
After the security check, the mother appears wan like a late winter moon.
The poet masks her childhood fear of separation by saying goodbye and repeatedly smiling.
Pablo Neruda asks everyone to count to twelve and remain still.
A pause without language, rush, or engines would create a strange shared moment.
In the imagined pause, fishermen would stop harming whales.
A salt gatherer would notice his injured hands.
Those preparing destructive wars would walk peacefully with their brothers.
The poet explicitly distinguishes quietness from total inactivity and death.
Silence may interrupt humanity's failure to understand itself and its threats of self-destruction.
Earth demonstrates that apparent stillness can later reveal life.
John Keats presents a beautiful thing as a lasting source of joy.
Beauty provides a quiet bower, peaceful sleep, health, and calm breathing.
People bind themselves to earthly life each day through a metaphorical flowery band.
Despondence, scarcity of noble people, gloomy days, and unhealthy ways darken human spirits.
Some form of beauty removes the pall of sadness from human spirits.
The poem names the sun, moon, trees, daffodils, clear streams, and musk roses as beautiful things.
The imagined grandeur of the mighty dead and lovely tales also sustain people.
Beauty is compared to an endless fountain of immortal drink flowing from heaven.
A poor rural family adds a roadside shed beside its old house to earn cash from passing traffic.
The stand offers wild berries, crooked-necked squash, and a mountain view.
Polished city traffic notices the stand mainly to complain about its painted signs.
The villagers want a share of the money that sustains prosperous cities.
The poet condemns official helpers as exploiters who destroy rural independence.
The family waits all day for the sound of a car stopping to buy something.
Cars stop only to turn around, ask directions, or request petrol that the stand does not sell.
The speaker's unbearable sympathy produces, then rejects, a wish to end the villagers' pain at one stroke.
Aunt Jennifer creates tigers that prance across an embroidered panel.
The bright topaz-coloured tigers inhabit a green world.
The embroidered tigers do not fear the men beneath the tree.
The tigers move with sleek, chivalric certainty.
Aunt Jennifer's fingers flutter nervously while working the wool.
The ivory needle feels difficult for Aunt Jennifer to pull.
The massive weight of the wedding band symbolises the burden of her marriage.
After Aunt Jennifer's death, her tigers will continue to prance proudly and fearlessly.
Charley, a thirty-one-year-old New Yorker, claims Grand Central Station has a third level.
His psychiatrist friend Sam calls the third level a waking-dream escape from modern insecurity.
On the third level, Charley sees gaslights, brass spittoons, old clothing, and an 1894 newspaper.
Charley tries to buy two tickets to Galesburg, Illinois, for himself and Louisa.
The clerk rejects Charley's modern currency and threatens to report it as counterfeit.
Charley buys old-style currency but cannot find the third level again.
Sam disappears after advising Charley to stop searching for the third level.
A first-day cover yields Sam's letter, postmarked July 18, 1894, describing his life in Galesburg.
Astrologers predict that the ten-day-old crown prince will die because of a tiger.
After becoming Maharaja, he forbids everyone else in Pratibandapuram from hunting tigers.
The Maharaja vows to kill one hundred tigers and personally kills the first seventy.
He avoids offending a British officer by sending diamond rings to the officer's wife.
He marries a princess from a state with many tigers and raises his total to ninety-nine.
The dewan secretly brings an old zoo tiger so the Maharaja can complete his count.
The Maharaja's shot misses the hundredth tiger, which hunters later kill to preserve his belief.
A sliver from a wooden toy tiger infects the Maharaja's hand, and he dies after surgery.

chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth

facts.text: Tishani Doshi travels to Antarctica aboard the Russian research vessel Akademik Shokalskiy.
The voyage begins in Madras and crosses nine time zones, six checkpoints, three oceans, and many ecosystems.
Antarctica preserves evidence of the ancient supercontinent Gondwana.
Gondwana centred roughly around present-day countries surrounding the Indian Ocean.
Antarctica's ice cores preserve ancient carbon records that help scientists study climate history.
The Students on Ice programme takes high-school students to polar regions to build environmental understanding.
Microscopic marine phytoplankton sustain the Southern Ocean food chain and absorb carbon during photosynthesis.
The group walks on sea ice above deep water near the Antarctic Circle and watches Crabeater seals.
Japanese surgeon Dr Sadao Hoki and his wife Hana find a wounded American prisoner washed ashore.
Sadao recognises the man as an enemy sailor but refuses to let a wounded person die untreated.
Sadao removes a bullet from the unconscious prisoner's back.
The household servants leave because they believe helping the enemy betrays Japan.
Sadao reports the prisoner to the General, who promises to send private assassins.
The General forgets his promise because he is preoccupied with his own health and dependence on Sadao.
Sadao gives the recovered prisoner a boat, food, clothing, and directions toward a nearby island.
When the prisoner's signal disappears, Sadao concludes that the escape succeeded.
Derry is a fourteen-year-old boy whose face is scarred by acid on one side.
Derry enters Mr Lamb's garden believing it to be empty.
Mr Lamb has a tin leg from the war and keeps his garden gate open.
Derry expects fear or pity because strangers comment on his scarred face.
Mr Lamb urges Derry to listen to bees, enjoy the world, and avoid shutting himself away.
Mr Lamb treats weeds and flowers as equally alive and valuable.
Derry defies his mother's objections and returns to help Mr Lamb.
Derry finds Mr Lamb dead after the old man falls from a ladder while picking crab apples.
The chapter combines autobiographical accounts by Zitkala-Sa and Bama.
At a Native American boarding school, Zitkala-Sa resists the compulsory cutting of her long hair.
Zitkala-Sa hides under a bed but is discovered, tied to a chair, and shingled.
In her culture, short hair is associated with mourners, cowards, or captured warriors.
As a child, Bama watches an elderly Dalit man carry a food packet by its string for a landlord.
Bama first laughs at the sight before her brother explains that untouchability causes the man's behaviour.
Bama becomes angry that caste prejudice denies dignity to people who labour for the upper castes.
Her brother advises her to study and progress, and academic success earns her respect.
